title: Secrets under wax
text: Herodotus says the exiled Demaratus scratched a warning on the wood of a writing tablet, then covered it with fresh wax so that the tablet appeared blank.
use: Greek warning of the Persian invasion.

title: A message on a shaved head
text: Herodotus also tells of Histiaeus tattooing a message on a slave's scalp and letting the hair grow back.
use: Used to signal a revolt against Persia.

title: Invisible inks
text: Pliny the Elder mentions plant sap that darkens when heated. Lemon juice, milk and later chemical inks work the same way, appearing only under heat or a reagent.
use: Revolutionary War spies and both World Wars used secret inks.

title: The Cardan grille
text: Girolamo Cardano proposed a card with holes. Letters written through the holes are surrounded with innocent words, so the page reads as an ordinary letter.
use: Diplomatic and private correspondence.

title: Bacon's two typefaces
text: Francis Bacon's biliteral cipher hides five-bit letters in the choice between two slightly different typefaces. It is an early binary code and an early form of steganography.
use: Described in The Advancement of Learning.

title: Pinpricks and newspaper ads
text: Tiny pinpricks under letters in a newspaper could spell out messages, and enciphered notes appeared openly in personal columns.
use: Private correspondents, including those in Le Figaro.

title: Microdots
text: Photographic reduction shrank a page to a dot the size of a full stop, which could be pasted into a letter. The FBI's J. Edgar Hoover famously called it the enemy's masterpiece of espionage.
use: German agents in the Second World War.

title: Null ciphers
text: An ordinary-looking message hides another in chosen letters, such as the first letter of each word. A wartime censor had to treat every odd phrasing with suspicion.
use: Spies and prisoners. Censors sometimes rephrased telegrams to destroy such messages.

title: Digital steganography
text: Changing the least significant bit of each colour value alters an image invisibly. Modern methods also hide data in audio, video and network timing.
use: Watermarking, privacy tools and malware command channels.

title: Printer tracking dots
text: The Electronic Frontier Foundation showed that many colour laser printers embed near-invisible yellow dots encoding a date and serial number.
use: A hidden channel built into everyday office equipment.

title: Torch signals
text: Polybius described torch signals that spelled out letters from a grid, turning distance signalling into something that could carry arbitrary text.
use: Greek military communication.

title: Couriers and pigeons
text: Messengers carried sealed letters for millennia. Homing pigeons flew messages over enemy lines, and were still in military use during the Second World War.
use: A coded message was found on a pigeon skeleton in a Surrey chimney in 2012.

title: Chappe's optical telegraph
text: Claude Chappe built towers with movable arms along chains of hilltops. Revolutionary France could send messages across the country in hours. Operators saw only code groups.
use: French government network.

title: The electric telegraph
text: Morse and Vail's system made messages nearly instant, but messages passed through clerks. That drove the growth of commercial codes and field ciphers.
use: Railways, commerce, and the American Civil War.

title: Cables cut and tapped
text: At the start of the First World War, Britain cut Germany's undersea cables, forcing traffic onto routes that Britain could read.
use: It led directly to the Zimmermann Telegram interception.

title: Radio and Morse
text: Radio reached ships and armies anywhere, but anyone could listen. Everything had to be enciphered, and vast listening networks grew up to record it.
use: Enigma traffic was sent this way.

title: Teleprinters
text: Machines sent five-bit characters automatically, allowing direct machine encryption by devices such as the Lorenz SZ 40.
use: German high command traffic.

title: Frequency hopping
text: Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil patented hopping between radio frequencies in a shared pattern, to make torpedo guidance hard to jam. The idea later became central to modern spread-spectrum radio.
use: Patent granted in 1942.

title: SIGSALY
text: A room-sized digital voice system used one-time key on phonograph records, letting Allied leaders talk securely across the Atlantic.
use: Churchill and Roosevelt's transatlantic calls.

title: Numbers stations and burst transmitters
text: Shortwave stations read out groups of digits to agents, who decoded them with one-time pads. Burst devices compressed messages into seconds to avoid direction finding.
use: Espionage, and some stations are still heard today.

title: Computer networks
text: Public-key cryptography made it possible for strangers on a shared network to set up a secret.
use: The foundation of secure internet commerce.

title: SSL and TLS
text: Web browsers began encrypting traffic automatically, and today most web pages travel over TLS using authenticated encryption.
use: HTTPS on most of the web.

title: End-to-end messaging
text: Protocols such as Signal's encrypt so that the service carrying the message cannot read it. Keys also change constantly, limiting the damage if one is stolen.
use: Billions of people use such messaging apps.

title: Quantum key distribution
text: Bennett and Brassard's 1984 protocol uses the physics of photons to detect eavesdropping during key exchange. In 2017 China's Micius satellite demonstrated it over intercontinental distances.
use: Research networks and specialist links.
